newsitem.title: GERMANY: German builders, employers to meet in talks.
newsitem.headline: German builders, employers to meet in talks.

text.p: Hopes grew that a damaging full-blown strike could be avoided in Germany's troubled construction industry on Tuesday as unions and employers agreed to high-level talks in a bid to settle their dispute.

No date has been set for the talks between employer and union leaders. But with time running out before a May 21 deadline when a strike ballot could be called, a meeting was expected to be held in the next few days.
Both sides had indicated their willingness to open fresh talks in the hope of averting the first large-scale construction industry strike since 1950.
Employers had offered the IG Bau union the chance for new talks and said negotiations could take place later this week.
The union responded with a positive answer as a union spokesman said IG Bau was also prepared for new talks.

But crucial differences remain between the sides in their dispute over the outcome of a controversial arbitration deal reached last week in which sick-pay benefits would be cut and workers would receive a pay increase below German inflation.

IG Bau has insisted workers receive full sick-pay benefits for the six-week period allowed under German law and rejected the arbitration decision that workers be paid at 80 percent for the first three weeks and at 100 percent for the balance.
The union also said it would not consider any new pay deal brokered by the arbitrator, the Christian Democrat politician Heiner Geissler, and that Geissler could attend the talks only as a moderator.
A vice president at the ZDB construction employer group, Wilhelm Kuechler, said on Tuesday any new talks would have to take place without pre-conditions.

Kuechler also said the union must put forward new proposals to find a solution to the issue of sick pay, one that has been at the forefront of German industry as it seeks to cut costs to remain competitive and also to combat high unemployment.
Other industry employer groups and major corporations such as industrial group Daimler-Benz AG have tried but failed to cut sick-pay benefits amid widespread union backlash.

IG Bau leader Klaus Wiesenhuegel said on Monday the union was prepared to compensate for full payment of sick-pay benefits but said it was "a matter of principle" to defend the rights of workers to sick pay.

The controversial arbitration deal calls for workers to receive a wage hike of 1.3 percent retroactive to April 1 and reducing Christmas bonus payments. German inflation was steady at 1.4 percent in April.

German construction minister Klaus Toepfer, speaking on German radio, called on Tuesday for a conciliation between the sides and said an industrial dispute would only cause further damage in an already weakened industry.

Analysts believe any strike would likely be limited since neither side can afford a prolonged dispute in a sector suffering from mass employment, with about 400,000 of its 1.3 million workers out of a job.
